a.xlink:title: Nebari should standardize the RWX capability and its acceptance criteria while allowing each infrastructure provider to supply the most suitable implementation.

The 2026-08-13 discussion added three more adverse data points, each qualified by the person raising it. Tyler Potts: EFS caps IOPS where S3 parallelises reads across Ray workers, and EFS can get expensive. Nick Byrne: data-engineering reads are metadata-heavy — a Parquet sidecar read repeatedly to skip irrelevant blobs — which is where EFS is said to degrade, but he flagged it explicitly as inherited folklore he has never tested. Vini Cerutti: Quansight benchmarked blob storage against EFS and concluded EFS was too slow, and Confluency moved off EFS to S3 for exactly that Parquet read/write pattern — but that is three to four years old and Nebari Classic era. None of it measures Elastic throughput mode, and none of it is about FSx for OpenZFS.

a.xlink:title: The single-writer ordering does not survive load. From one to four concurrent writers Longhorn degrades 2.2-2.6x and FSx 1.7-2.7x, while EFS Elastic is flat (1.1-1.2x) — so by four writers the three converge and EFS is fastest on environment creation (72 s, against Longhorn 83 s and FSx 99 s). The mechanism is structural: Longhorn funnels every client through one share-manager pod on one node and FSx is capped by its provisioned throughput tier, both fixed budgets divided among clients, where EFS scales capacity on demand. Nebari is a multi-user platform and four writers is a small cluster; where the crossover sits beyond four is unmeasured and is the most decision-relevant gap left in the performance evidence.

a.xlink:title: A core platform requirement should define observable behavior, not mandate one storage product.
Longhorn remains necessary for providers that lack a suitable managed RWX abstraction.

At one writer Longhorn RWX matches FSx on extraction, clone and checkout and is 1.8x faster on environment creation (32.0 s against 56.3 s). Moving `/shared` to a managed filesystem is therefore a measurable regression on the workload the pack cares most about — the map already says a managed filesystem buys operational simplification rather than speed, and that is now confirmed with a price attached rather than assumed to be zero. The advantage inverts under concurrency, per concurrency inverts the ranking.

a.xlink:title: A single Longhorn implementation on every provider would reduce variation in deployment and support procedures.

The honest unit of Longhorn's operational cost is per cluster and per operator, not per provider. Removing it from AWS does not remove it from the project while Hetzner needs it, but it does remove it from every AWS cluster and everyone on call for one. Priced under the operations gate.

a.xlink:title: The cost gate asks for operator overhead as a line item inside it, and the unit is hours per cluster per month because that is how the burden scales. Built from the runbooks NIC ships and the incidents observed during the benchmark — drains and node maintenance ~3 h, incident response ~2 h, upgrades, capacity tuning, backup drift checks and maintaining the expertise — Longhorn totals ~9.3 h/mo against ~2.3 h/mo residual on a managed filesystem, a delta of ~7 h/mo/cluster. It is left in hours on purpose: converting it needs a loaded rate, and whoever owns the staffing budget has that rate. Two consequences do not need one — the delta is flat, so ten Longhorn clusters is ~70 h/mo, roughly half an FTE; and being flat it weighs heaviest on small clusters, where the whole infrastructure bill is $231/mo. This is an estimate, not a measurement, and it is the number most worth firming up: tag storage-related toil in on-call's tracker for a quarter. It is here because leaving it out prices it at zero, which is the one value known to be wrong.

a.xlink:title: Getting the benchmark cluster into a testable state hit the drain problem directly (2026-08-14). A routine node-group disk resize on `jamesolds-dev` failed three times, roughly 29 minutes each, with `PodEvictionFailure`: Longhorn's `instance-manager` PDB reported zero allowed disruptions while it held a volume's last replica, under the default `node-drain-policy: block-if-contains-last-replica`. Neither surge headroom nor detaching the workload cleared it, and the roll completed only with `--force`. So routine node maintenance on a Longhorn cluster means deliberately relaxing a data-safety setting first, which is the runbook's five steps meeting a real cluster. Two adjacent findings came with it: `max_nodes` must exceed `min_nodes` or an EKS node-group update has no room to launch a replacement before draining, which makes any PDB unsatisfiable (worth a NIC validation, and independent of Longhorn); and `keycloak-db-primary` sits at zero allowed disruptions too, so the cluster has a second, unrelated reason a node cannot be drained — relevant to HA is not durability and to the CNPG `instances: 2-3` discussion. The `max_nodes` gap is a NIC validation we will add, and the drain procedure can be automated further than it is — but the burden itself survives both fixes, because what the operator is doing is evicting replicas from a storage system whose safety setting has to be relaxed for maintenance to proceed. Better tooling shortens that; it does not remove the class of work.

a.xlink:title: Longhorn keeps replicas under `/var/lib/longhorn` on the node root disk and reserves 25% of it, so NIC's 20 GB default leaves ~2.4 GB schedulable. A 20 GiB RWX volume therefore goes straight to `faulted`/`detached`, no share-manager pod is created, and consuming pods sit in `ContainerCreating` until they time out, with no error naming disk space (observed 2026-08-14; fixed by setting `disk_size: 100`). RWX is the only capability Longhorn is retained for on AWS under the split shape, and it is broken on a default-shaped cluster. This is a NIC bug and will be fixed in NIC — raise the default when Longhorn is enabled, or fail validation up front — so it is not an argument that Longhorn cannot work here. What it is evidence of is how much Longhorn-specific knowledge the integration silently assumes: the failure names no cause, and diagnosing it means knowing about the 25% reserve on `/var/lib/longhorn`.
